items.title: Rich Hickey argues LLMs are automation not tools, but others say using AI well requires skill and human judgment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI is a tool and using it well takes skill
items.summary:
Rich Hickey contends that large language models (LLMs) function as automation rather than tools because they cannot be directly wielded by humans. However, others argue that LLMs can be wielded with skill, requiring users to direct, interpret, and correct outputs much like traditional tools. They emphasize that unpredictability does not disqualify LLMs as tools, and that automation can be a feature within tools, citing examples like compilers and spreadsheets.

The debate also touches on the importance of human intention and expertise in using LLMs effectively, with users engaging in feedback loops to refine outputs. Concerns about AI anthropomorphizing and the potential to avoid intellectual work are addressed, highlighting that the key distinction lies in whether users wield AI with understanding and oversight or delegate tasks without adequate control. This perspective suggests a more practical approach to AI as a tool rather than dismissing it outright as automation.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate AI models can embed hidden capabilities via encrypted backdoors resistant to elicitation and interpretation [ ~ ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: AI models can provably hide arbitrary capabilities
items.summary: Researchers have shown that AI models can embed hidden capabilities using encrypted neural networks activated only by secret triggers, making these capabilities provably difficult to detect or interpret even with full access to model weights. They implemented these backdoor attacks in PyTorch and tested their resistance to various elicitation methods on a chemical reaction prediction task, highlighting limitations in current capability evaluation approaches. This work raises concerns about the reliability of audits designed to detect dangerous model behaviors before deployment and underscores the need for improved defenses against such hidden functionalities.

items.title: Intel launches D270 GPU AI accelerator with up to 480 GB LPDDR5X memory for inference-optimized data center workloads [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Intel D270 GPU AI Accelerator–Up to 480 GB LPDDR5X
items.summary:
Intel has introduced the D270 GPU, designed specifically for AI inference in data centers, offering up to 480 GB of LPDDR5X memory and 32 Xe3P cores to support agentic AI workloads. The GPU targets long-context, high-concurrency AI applications, emphasizing power efficiency and compatibility with standard PCIe 5.0 infrastructure.

The D270 GPU aims to handle larger AI model contexts and more concurrent sessions without requiring high bandwidth memory or liquid cooling, making it suitable for enterprise AI, SaaS, and sovereign cloud deployments. It supports popular AI frameworks like PyTorch and vLLM, focusing on efficient token serving and scalable inference within existing data center power and rack constraints.

items.title: Agent37 launches low-cost agent sandboxes with free plan enabled by optimized CPU/RAM use and non-hyperscaler hosting [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Launch HN: Agent37 (YC F26) – Low-cost agent sandboxes for running agents
items.summary:
Agent37, a startup founded by a former Amazon engineer, has launched low-cost sandboxes for running AI agents, offering a free plan made possible by infrastructure optimizations. The company reduces costs by managing CPU and RAM usage patterns specific to agent workloads, avoiding hyperscaler cloud providers in favor of vendors like Hetzner and OVH, and using gVisor technology to share resources efficiently across hosts.

The free sandboxes cost approximately $0.05 to $0.10 per user per month, enabling over 90% of new signups to use the free tier for hosting personal AI agent code such as Hermes, Openclaw, and Claude. Agent37 targets developers building messaging agents and aims to provide a cost-effective platform tailored to the niche requirements of agent harness workloads.

items.summary: Kevin Kelly's 2016 book The Inevitable predicted that by 2026, Google's main product would shift from search to AI, driven by advances in cloud-based AI and deep learning. Kelly highlighted Google's strategy of using search data to train its AI systems, suggesting that search serves as a means to improve AI rather than the other way around. The predictions also anticipated an oligopoly of a few large cloud-based AI providers and the rise of specialized AI software.

items.title: Character.ai files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy to pursue court-supervised sale amid legal and operational challenges [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Character.ai files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy
items.summary:
Character.ai has initiated a voluntary Chapter 11 bankruptcy process to enable a court-supervised sale of the company, aiming to maximize value for stakeholders while continuing platform operations. The company cited significant legal, regulatory, and operational difficulties over the past year as reasons for this decision.

The Character.ai platform remains active and accessible, with subscriptions continuing unchanged for now. The sale process is expected to conclude by late November or early December 2026, and the company hopes to find a buyer that will allow the platform to continue operating; otherwise, it will be wound down. User data protections and privacy policies remain in place during this process.

items.summary:
This position paper examines the limitations of current faithfulness metrics used in Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to measure how well explanations align with machine learning models. The authors identify five major shortcomings that hinder rigorous quantification of faithfulness, which affects the trustworthiness of XAI methods often used more as debugging tools than for building user trust.

The paper discusses how oversimplification in XAI explanations leads to misalignment with the underlying models, causing unfaithfulness or infidelity. It proposes four research avenues aimed at addressing these challenges to enhance the reliability and computational feasibility of faithfulness metrics in feature importance explanations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12493v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) tools have often been presented as methods to increase trust in machine learning models by making aspects of their algorithms more human-understandable. However, evidence accumulated over the last decade points to an overall failure of this objective, instead promoting overreliance on incorrect predictions, which can subsequently lead to algorithmic aversion. Rather, XAI appears to function primarily as a debugging tool, useful for obtaining anecdotal insights into, for example, features learned by the model. One of the main issues underlying this limitation is that XAI methods often oversimplify the inner workings of the model, resulting in misalignment between the explanation and the model itself - a behavior referred to as unfaithfulness or infidelity. Faithfulness can be interpreted as the degree of approximation between an explanation and the model. Computing faithfulness in a rigorous manner would thus make it possible to quantify one of the various elements of trustworthiness of an explanation. However, existing metrics present significant limitations, making this quantification either infeasible or computationally expensive. In this position paper, we outline five major shortcomings of current faithfulness metrics and propose four possible avenues for research to bolster their reliability.

items.title: EliteTable uses large language models to guide self-improving program search for control policies, showing performance gains across six Gymnasium tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EliteTable: Self-Improving Program Search for Executable Control Policies
items.summary: EliteTable is a program-search algorithm that leverages large language models and a fixed-capacity table of high-scoring solutions to generate, edit, and remix candidate programs for control tasks. It was tested on six Gymnasium control environments with multiple generations and candidate slots, showing median score improvements in most tasks and transfer of gains to new episodes in some cases. While CartPole-v1 reached peak scores early, other tasks like BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3 improved without hitting targets, and Acrobot-v1 showed mixed results. Further comparisons and ablation studies are needed to clarify EliteTable's relative effectiveness and component contributions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12536v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: EliteTable is a self-improving program-search algorithm guided by large language models (LLMs) that uses a fixed-capacity table of high-scoring solutions to guide new proposals, edits of existing solutions, and remixes of several solutions. Performance was evaluated across six Gymnasium control tasks, each with ten generations and fifty candidate slots per generation. Each task was evaluated across ten independently initialized searches. Candidate-score medians rose between the first and final generations in all six tasks, and selected-winner search-score medians rose in five. In CartPole-v1, the selected winner reached the search-score ceiling in the first generation of all ten searches. All ten paired held-out endpoints improved in four of the six tasks. BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3 improved without reaching their reporting targets. Six of ten Acrobot-v1 searches declined on held-out episodes, and the median paired change was negative. The results document improvement during program search and the transfer of selected-winner gains to new episodes in some tasks. Comparisons and ablations are needed to establish EliteTable's relative performance and the contributions of its components.

items.title: Controlled study finds Monte Carlo Tree Search 2.88% less effective than randomized-restart list scheduling for DAG workflow scheduling under equal computational budgets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Equal-Budget Monte Carlo Tree Search versus Randomized-Restart List Scheduling for DAG Workflows: A Controlled Equal-Budget Computational Study
items.summary: Researchers conducted a controlled computational study comparing Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) and randomized-restart list scheduling for directed-acyclic-graph (DAG) workflow scheduling, ensuring both methods used the same number of candidate schedule evaluations. The study found that at a budget of 2048 schedules, MCTS performed 2.88% worse than the randomized restarts, with results validated by an independent checker across 768 schedules. The deficit was not due to insufficient budget, and performance varied by workflow structure, with restarts outperforming on sparse irregular workflows and no significant difference on regular or dense workflows. The study was limited to synthetic domains with up to 32 tasks and 8 processors, and results may not generalize to larger budgets or real-world scenarios.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) is often proposed for scheduling directed-acyclic-graph (DAG) workflows, yet most studies never run the comparison that could refute it - giving a much simpler method the same search effort. We run that comparison under a controlled protocol. All arms receive an identical budget - the same number of candidate schedules built and evaluated: an MCTS scheduling method, preregistered as the main arm; a randomized-restart list scheduler with no search tree as the control; and a textbook-UCT MCTS arm as a registered follow-up on the same domain. The analysis plan was locked before data collection; an independent checker confirmed all 768 confirmation-stage schedules valid with correct finish times. At the main budget of 2048 evaluated schedules, MCTS is 2.88% worse than the restarts (95% CI [-3.62%,-2.15%]; the 72 of 96 held-out instances with positive baseline-relative headroom). The deficit is not budget starvation: on the separate exploration pool restarts self-improve by 1.85% where MCTS gains 0.24%, and 700 of 720 of MCTS's first results are merely the warm start it was handed. The studied selection rule locks deterministically onto the first-expanded child, keeping its trials correlated while restarts draw gains from the tails; the causal link to makespan remains an inference. A structural map locates where the tree stops paying: restarts win on sparse irregular workflows, no difference is detectable on regular layered ones, and dense ones leave no room to improve. Swapping the rule for textbook UCT removes most of the deficit (-0.26%, 95% CI [-0.71%,+0.23%]) without reversing its sign. Results are confined to a controlled synthetic domain (N in {8,16,32} tasks, 2-8 processors, budgets up to 2048); we make no claim about larger budgets.

items.title: Researchers propose EvoSyn, a multi-agent framework for agentic data synthesis that adapts and expands generation space using learner feedback to improve task success in interactive AI agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Know What You Don't Know: Agentic Data Synthesis by Evolving Generation Space for Closed-Loop Learning
items.summary:
Researchers introduce EvoSyn, a multi-agent system designed to enhance synthetic data generation for interactive agents by using learner feedback to adapt and expand the synthesis space. This framework organizes synthesis around a revisable state that specifies interaction factors and allocates synthesis effort, enabling targeted improvements and discovery of new controllable factors.

EvoSyn employs specialized agents to translate feedback into synthesis revisions, with a Designer directing synthesis and a Planner executing experience generation. Experiments on $\tau^2$-Bench and CAR-Bench demonstrate that EvoSyn improves average task success by 13.3 points over leading baselines while producing higher-quality and more structurally diverse synthetic experiences, addressing limitations in existing methods that struggle to close the feedback-to-decision gap in data synthesis for learning agents.

EvoSyn employs specialized agents to translate feedback into synthesis revisions, with a Designer directing synthesis and a Planner executing experience generation. Experiments on $\tau^2$-Bench and CAR-Bench demonstrate that EvoSyn improves average task success by 13.3 points over leading baselines while producing higher-quality and more structurally diverse synthetic experiences, addressing limitations in existing methods that struggle to close the feedback-to-decision gap in data synthesis for learning agents.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12593v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The continued improvement of large language models increasingly depends on synthetic experience, yet effective data synthesis for interactive agents requires not only executable and verifiable trajectories, but also interactions that provide learning value for the current task agent. Existing methods increasingly incorporate environment feedback, data validation, or learner failures, but still face a feedback-to-decision gap: observed weaknesses do not directly specify how future synthesis should change, or whether they can be represented by the current synthesis space. To address this gap, we propose EvoSyn, a learning-feedback-driven multi-agent framework that organizes synthesis around a revisable state specifying what interaction factors can be deliberately generated and where synthesis effort should be allocated. A role-specialized multi-agent system translates learner feedback into synthesis revisions, while a Designer allocates synthesis directions and a Planner grounds them into executable experience. This process enables within-space adaptation toward weak or under-covered regions and synthesis-space expansion that promotes newly discovered factors into explicit generation controls. Experiments on $\tau^2$-Bench and CAR-Bench show that EvoSyn improves average task success by 13.3 points over the strongest synthesis baseline, while producing higher-quality and structurally broader synthetic experience and discovering controllable factors missed without learner feedback.

items.title: SpireBench evaluates long-horizon strategic play of 20 large language models in Slay the Spire, showing models match average humans but lag behind experts over extended runs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SpireBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Strategic Play of Agentic Models with Slay the Spire
items.summary:
Researchers introduce SpireBench, a benchmark where large language models play the full commercial deck-building game Slay the Spire to assess long-term strategic reasoning. Testing 20 models at the game's highest difficulty reveals that while frontier models outperform heuristic baselines and match average human players, they fall behind expert players as game runs lengthen, particularly due to misjudging risk and health management during fights.

The study finds that models rely partly on prior knowledge of the game and do not improve from in-game memories, which tend to be inaccurate and overly cautious. SpireBench is the first benchmark to provide models with the complete original game and offers tools to analyze where and why agentic models fail in long-horizon tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12596v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic large language models now tackle complex tasks, yet strategic reasoning over long horizons is under-studied: most agentic benchmarks are short and episodic, and performance on long tasks is hard to dissect into stored knowledge, reasoning and luck. We introduce SpireBench, in which models play the complete commercial deck-builder Slay the Spire (StS), where early decisions decide long-term success. Across 20 large language models (LLMs) at the game's highest difficulty, frontier models beat heuristic baselines and match the average human player but remain far behind experts. This gap widens as the run lengthens: the strongest models win the first act as often as experts, then fall behind. What separates strong models from weak is how well they play each fight; all of them misjudge risk over a run, preserving health rather than spending it to grow stronger. A comprehensive, self-consistent renaming of every game term shows that part of their performance rests on prior knowledge of the game, and models do not improve from the memories they write across runs, which are often wrong and overly cautious. Our harness is the first to give a model the complete original game, and we compare it with existing harnesses. Overall, SpireBench offers an unsaturated long-horizon benchmark with tools to locate where and why agents fail.

items.title: Researchers introduce Behavioral Self-Rewarding to refine reinforcement learning rewards for software engineering agents, improving debugging quality without new environment interactions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents
items.summary: Researchers propose Behavioral Self-Rewarding (BSR), a method that enhances reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards by enabling software engineering agents to judge and compare their own debugging trajectories. BSR refines binary pass/fail rewards into bounded auxiliary rewards based on pairwise preferences, providing additional supervision from existing data without requiring new environment interactions. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench-Live demonstrate consistent performance improvements using Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B models, supporting the use of the policy's own comparative judgments as a complementary learning signal for training software engineering agents.

Experiments on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench-Live demonstrate consistent performance improvements using Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B models, supporting the use of the policy's own comparative judgments as a complementary learning signal for training software engineering agents.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides reliable supervision for software engineering agents through executable tests, but binary rewards fail to distinguish trajectories with substantially different debugging quality. We investigate whether the current policy can judge its own trajectories and use these judgments to improve task performance without a separately trained reward model. To this end, we introduce Behavioral Self-Rewarding (BSR), a reward-refinement method that reuses the policy to compare observable debugging behavior among trajectories from the same task with the same verifier outcome. BSR aggregates pairwise preferences into task-local scores and converts them into bounded auxiliary rewards, introducing reward contrast while preserving the verifier-defined pass/fail ordering. This provides additional supervision from already-collected trajectories without requiring new environment interactions. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench-Live show consistent improvements across the evaluated Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B configurations, supporting using the policy's own comparative judgments as a complementary learning signal for training software engineering agents.

items.originalTitle: CLEAT: Learning Value-Guided Clarification for Interactive Agents
items.summary:
Researchers present CLEAT (CLarification through valuE-guided Agent co-Training), a framework that co-trains a clarification-value controller and task policy to help large language model agents ask useful questions and make better decisions when user goals are unstated. CLEAT measures the utility of clarification through paired rollouts and adapts its guidance as the agent learns, achieving top scores on ten evaluation settings across four benchmarks with the Qwen3-4B model.

CLEAT improves task policy performance even without the controller at inference and shows significant gains over strong baselines, including 13.2 and 6.5 percentage points improvements on UserGym Travel and IN3 underspecification judgment accuracy, respectively. The approach addresses the challenge of interactive intent alignment by enabling agents to effectively use clarifications to handle incomplete information and evolving policies.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12655v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents can execute increasingly complex tasks, but effective assistance also requires aligning their actions with goals and constraints that users may leave unstated. We study this problem as interactive intent alignment through clarification. Yet clarification is useful only when the agent can turn the answer into better decisions. As training changes how the agent handles incomplete information and uses additional answers, the same clarification can become more or less useful. We introduce CLEAT (CLarification through valuE-guided Agent co-Training), a framework that co-trains a clarification-value controller and the task policy from shared interaction outcomes. We formulate residual query value to measure the task utility gained by asking rather than proceeding under the current policy, and estimate it through paired rollouts from the same interaction history. These paired returns train the controller to predict clarification value and the task policy to select useful questions and act on the answers. The controller guides subsequent rollout collection, while outcomes from the updated agent provide new value labels that allow clarification guidance to adapt as the agent learns. With Qwen3-4B, CLEAT achieves the highest mean score in all ten evaluation settings across four benchmarks. Gains over the strongest baseline reach 13.2 and 6.5 percentage points on UserGym Travel and IN3 underspecification judgment accuracy, respectively. Ablations show that co-training improves the task policy even when the controller is removed at inference, while adapting clarification guidance to the evolving policy yields further gains.

items.title: Researchers introduce MagicBeanStalk, a recursive data synthesis algorithm that generates policy- and budget-calibrated training problems to overcome the zero-advantage trap in RLVR datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MagicBeanStalk: Escaping the RLVR Zero Advantage Trap with Recursive Data Synthesis
items.summary:
Researchers identify that a large open-source math corpus used in reinforcement learning with verifiable reasoning (RLVR) largely falls into a zero-advantage trap, where most problems are either always solved or always failed for a fixed policy and rollout budget. To address this, they develop MagicBeanStalk, an algorithm that recursively synthesizes new training problems calibrated to the target policy and training budget, preserving the reasoning structure of seed problems.

Testing across eight math benchmarks, continual RLVR training on MagicBeanStalk-generated problems improves model performance significantly more than training on the full original corpus or its filtered subsets. The approach also synthesizes over 14,000 verifiable finance problems from 340 solutions, yielding notable accuracy gains on finance benchmarks SecQue and FinanceBench.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12659v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data-centric scaling of RLVR has focused on collecting or generating verifiable training problems. However, corpus size alone does not determine whether the dataset provides a useful learning signal for a target policy. To guide the synthesis of effective RLVR data, we experimentally characterize dataset effectiveness as a function of its problems, the target policy, and the training rollout budget. Under this characterization, we show that a large open-source math corpus pooled from widely used RLVR datasets falls almost entirely into a zero-advantage trap: for a fixed target policy and rollout budget, roughly 88% of its problems are solved in every rollout or failed in every rollout. Filtering concentrates what remains, but it can only select, discarding the hard problems. Effective synthetic problems should therefore require the reasoning operations and compositions required to solve those hard problems. Yet their difficulty must be calibrated, so that some rollouts succeed, some fail, and at least one correct solution fits within the training budget. Prompting a teacher to vary hard problems directly does not achieve this. Guided by these empirical principles, we introduce MagicBeanStalk, a top-down decomposition and bottom-up recursive data-synthesis algorithm that grows seed problems into families of substantively new, policy- and budget-calibrated training problems while preserving the seeds' reasoning blueprints. Across 8 math benchmarks, continual RLVR on MagicBeanStalk problems improves gpt-oss-120b from 61.2 to 69.8 (+8.6) and DeepSeek v4Flash from 72.4 to 77.9 (+5.4) on a 16K-token budget. Training on the full 78K source corpus improves by only +1.1 and its best filtered real data subset by +5.8. In finance, we synthesize over 14K verifiable problems from only 340 solutions and improve over base by 6.9 and 2.4 points on SecQue and FinanceBench, respectively.

items.title: Researchers develop LLM-driven pipeline to automate construction of hierarchical hardware knowledge graphs from datasheets, achieving 98.8% property faithfulness across diverse components [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Faithful and Complete LLM-Assisted Automated Construction of Hierarchical Hardware Knowledge Graphs
items.summary:
Researchers present an automated pipeline using large language models (LLMs) to convert hardware datasheets into hierarchical knowledge graphs that organize engineering specifications for component selection and system integration. The approach uses chunk-based extraction, hierarchical routing, and iterative refinement to preserve source provenance and reduce context size, improving accuracy over one-shot methods.

The framework was evaluated on 20 hardware datasheets covering various component types and lengths, achieving 98.8% property faithfulness compared to 76.1% for a baseline method and covering 83.6% of baseline properties fully. These knowledge graphs provide more reliable and comprehensive engineering data to support hardware design and verification, reducing risks of overlooked constraints and errors.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12762v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hardware datasheets contain engineering specifications essential for component selection, system integration, and hardware compatibility verification. However, manual inspection is tedious and error-prone because datasheets are lengthy and heterogeneous, with dense information fragmented across tables, figures, and text. Although large language models (LLMs) can automate this process, na\"ive one-shot processing omits relevant specifications even when the document fits within the model's context window. We present an automated LLM-driven pipeline that transforms hardware datasheets into general-purpose hierarchical hardware knowledge graphs through chunk-based property extraction, hierarchical routing, and iterative refinement. The framework uses LLMs for information extraction and semantic reasoning while preserving source provenance and applying graph updates through validated instructions and deterministic local execution. This staged design reduces per-query context and maintains traceable intermediate representations. The resulting knowledge graphs provide semantically organized, source-grounded hardware properties for downstream retrieval and reasoning. We evaluate the framework on 20 hardware datasheets spanning diverse component types and document lengths. We assess property faithfulness and introduce inter-graph completeness to measure relative semantic coverage without exhaustive ground truth. Our framework achieves 98.8% property faithfulness compared with 76.1% for the one-shot baseline, while fully covering 83.6% of faithful baseline properties; in the reverse direction, the baseline fully covers only 10.5% of ours. These improvements provide more reliable and comprehensive engineering information for downstream hardware design and verification, reducing the risk of overlooked constraints and incorrect decisions.

items.title: Researchers propose distilled optimal transport method to align pretrained unimodal encoders using 100–500 paired examples amid abundant unpaired data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Representation Alignment from a Few Paired Data via Distilled Optimal Transport
items.summary: Researchers introduce a method that aligns two independently pretrained unimodal encoders with only 100 to 500 paired examples, leveraging abundant unpaired data on either side. Their approach represents each data point by its similarity to paired anchors, aligns the modalities via an entropic optimal transport problem with marginal constraints to mitigate hubness, and distills the alignment into lightweight encoders for inductive correspondence. The method requires pairing only for anchor points, allowing unpaired data to be drawn independently from each modality's distribution. Evaluations on image-text and molecule-text alignment tasks demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing methods on datasets including Flickr30k, MS-COCO, and ChEBI-20 at comparable anchor budgets.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aligning two independently pretrained unimodal encoders typically demands millions of paired examples. In this paper, we study the regime where only $N \sim 100$--$500$ pairs are available, while unpaired data on either side is abundant. Our method expresses every representation by its similarities to the $N$ paired anchors, which places both modalities in a common coordinate system; matches the two point clouds with a single entropic optimal transport problem solved over the entire pool, whose marginal constraints counteract the hubness that defeats nearest-neighbor matching; and distills the resulting plan into two lightweight encoders, so that the correspondence becomes inductive. We additionally put this marginal constraint in relation with the one-step hub corrections of the bilingual lexicon induction literature. Pairing is required only for the anchors: the unpaired collections may be drawn independently from the two marginals, so that no item outside the anchor set needs to have both of its modalities observed. We evaluate on image-text and molecule-text alignment, where our method outperforms existing approaches at the same anchor budget on Flickr30k, MS-COCO and ChEBI-20.

items.title: Researchers introduce EvoBelief, a self-evolving world model for LLM agents that updates environment knowledge through falsifiable hypotheses to improve task performance across benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: EvoBelief: Falsifiable World Models for Self-Improving LLM Agents
items.summary:
EvoBelief is a new approach for large language model (LLM) agents that evolves their beliefs about environment dynamics during deployment by forming and validating falsifiable hypotheses. Unlike traditional methods that update model parameters, EvoBelief maintains a frozen language model and updates rules linked to evidence, allowing agents to adapt to changes and improve predictions and planning.

The system was tested on four benchmarks including ALFWorld, MiniGrid, and DiscoveryWorld's Reactor Lab, showing significant improvements in success rates and the ability to revise stale rules and discover quantitative laws. EvoBelief demonstrated up to 31.3% higher success than comparable frozen models and completed tasks that baseline methods could not, highlighting its potential for self-improvement through testable and revisable environment knowledge.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12789v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-evolving LLM agents typically improve how they act through accumulated experience, reflection, or skills. Yet even procedurally capable agents can fail when their beliefs about environment dynamics are incomplete, incorrect, or outdated. We study a complementary axis of self-evolution: evolving those beliefs during deployment. Such beliefs can support multiple tasks, but incorrect ones can also propagate across them. We introduce EvoBelief, a self-evolving world model that represents environment knowledge as falsifiable hypotheses. Unexpected outcomes and decision-relevant unknowns trigger hypothesis formation. Later observations and controlled experiments provide independent validation before a rule can guide predictions or plans within its supported scope. Counterexamples narrow or retire rules as the environment changes. The language model remains frozen, and each rule remains linked to its evidence and the decisions it changes. Across four benchmarks spanning static dynamics, hidden drift, and scientific discovery, EvoBelief improves task performance and reuses learned rules across tasks. On ALFWorld without actor-side transition memory, it improves success over the matched Frozen World Model by 23.9% and 31.3% with Claude Haiku 4.5 and GPT-5.4, respectively. On MiniGrid, it revises stale rules and recovers after unannounced dynamics changes. In DiscoveryWorld's Reactor Lab, it discovers and validates quantitative laws, completing 83.3% of Normal-tier and 58.3% of Challenge-tier instances, versus 0% for each evaluated baseline. These results demonstrate self-improvement through testable, revisable environment knowledge rather than model-parameter updates.

items.title: VEPA: Verified Evolving Formal Policy for Lifelong LLM Agent Guardrails [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: VEPA: Verified Evolving Formal Policy for Lifelong LLM Agent Guardrails
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate over sensitive resources, such as private documents and mutable system states, which can create serious safety and security risks. Runtime guardrails should therefore make inspectable, reproducible, and deterministic allow or refuse decisions before potentially irreversible agent actions are executed. However, safety and security requirements are rarely complete before deployment, so guardrails need to keep adapting as new risks emerge. Existing adaptive guardrails learn from deployment experience, but they usually apply safety policies through LLM inference, which can lead to inconsistent decisions and ambiguous policy interpretations. Formal guardrails, on the other hand, enforce policies deterministically, but they usually rely on pre-deployment or task-specific policies and have no mechanism to adapt to newly observed risks. We introduce VEPA, a framework for the verified evolution of formal agent guardrails. VEPA represents the guardrail as a formal policy of executable symbolic rules over typed agent events. During deployment, we use an LLM guided by deployment feedback to propose policy patches that fix newly observed failures while preserving previously correct behavior. Then, a deterministic verifier only accepts policies that are structurally valid and conflict-free. Finally, an evidence-aware authority layer activates a verified rule only when it has enough supporting evidence, so uncertain updates cannot directly affect guardrail decisions. Across ASSEBench-Safety, ASSEBench-Security, and ATBench, VEPA consistently outperforms baselines while expanding the scope of deterministic formal-policy enforcement. These gains also hold under more challenging deployment conditions, including mixed streams, corrupted feedback, and longer horizons.

However, safety and security requirements are rarely complete before deployment, so guardrails need to keep adapting as new risks emerge. Existing adaptive guardrails learn from deployment experience, but they usually apply safety policies through LLM inference, which can lead to inconsistent decisions and ambiguous policy interpretations. Formal guardrails, on the other hand, enforce policies deterministically, but they usually rely on pre-deployment or task-specific policies and have no mechanism to adapt to newly observed risks. We introduce VEPA, a framework for the verified evolution of formal agent guardrails. VEPA represents the guardrail as a formal policy of executable symbolic rules over typed agent events. During deployment, we use an LLM guided by deployment feedback to propose policy patches that fix newly observed failures while preserving previously correct behavior. Then, a deterministic verifier only accepts policies that are structurally valid and conflict-free. Finally, an evidence-aware authority layer activates a verified rule only when it has enough supporting evidence, so uncertain updates cannot directly affect guardrail decisions. Across ASSEBench-Safety, ASSEBench-Security, and ATBench, VEPA consistently outperforms baselines while expanding the scope of deterministic formal-policy enforcement. These gains also hold under more challenging deployment conditions, including mixed streams, corrupted feedback, and longer horizons.

items.title: Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy in Multi-Agent Coding Systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy in Multi-Agent Coding Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12822v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used to solve coding tasks by coordinating agents that share code and plans. These agents are often optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) using automated evaluators, but bypassing evaluation can earn reward without producing a genuine solution. Prior work has largely treated reward hacking as a single-agent failure. In this work, we show that a reward-hacking strategy elicited in one agent can propagate to others and affect system coordination. Across four open-weight backbones, coding RL elicits and amplifies reward hacking in two settings: explicit mechanism descriptions in the system prompt and mid-training that models upstream exposure to facts about the coding environment. Using post-RL agents from the mid-training setting as sources, we observe propagation through code and shared memory, and across roles through natural-language plans. Even agents based on small open-weight models induce reward hacking in stronger closed-weight targets. On hard tasks, propagation can intensify along a transmission chain after the original source leaves as the code acquires more persuasive justifications. We also theoretically analyze conditions under which reward hacking amplifies, persists, or decays across agent interactions. Beyond propagation, reward hacking can bias task routing toward reward-hacking agents and survive candidate aggregation. As potential mitigations, we evaluate code review by the coder or a separate verifier, both of which reduce delivered hacks. Together, these results establish reward hacking as a transmissible strategy whose effects extend beyond the agent in which it first emerges.

items.title: Neural networks are more modular than single neurons suggest [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Neural networks are more modular than single neurons suggest
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12842v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural networks routinely develop representations in which individual neurons contribute to multiple distinct functions, leading to the widespread view that such networks lack modular organization. We challenge this conclusion by introducing a formally nested hierarchy of modularity: unit-level, which requires distinct computations to occupy disjoint neurons; orthogonal, which asks whether a rotation reveals functionally independent subspaces; and linear, which asks whether a bounded linear map can separate task-relevant computations into independent subspaces. We develop a unified framework for learning decompositions at each level and evaluating them causally through selective ablation. Across vision models, language models and multi-task Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), we find that networks which lack unit-level modularity nonetheless often exhibit clear functional modularity at the subspace level. In vision and language models, content versus style and syntax versus semantics respectively dissociate under subspace ablation despite sharing overlapping populations of neurons. These learned subspaces also align differentially with brain data, with content and style subspaces predicting higher and lower visual cortex respectively, and semantic subspaces outperforming syntactic ones in predicting language cortex activity. In RNNs trained on multiple cognitive tasks and previously shown to lack modular structure, our decomposition recovers sharp double dissociations between tasks. The absence of unit-level modularity frequently coexists with clear subspace-level modularity across domains, enabling targeted intervention on specific computations even in networks where no individual neuron is specialized, with broad implications for mechanistic interpretability and for understanding functional organization in both biological and artificial neural systems.

items.title: Towards Defining, Measuring, and Leveraging Creativity in AI Applications [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Towards Defining, Measuring, and Leveraging Creativity in AI Applications
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12845v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite extensive research, computational creativity still lacks a conceptually grounded, practically relevant, and empirically applicable formal definition across contexts such as art, scientific research, and games. Existing approaches to creativity often focus on proposing informal conceptual definitions without providing formal computational concepts. Alternatively, they propose formal definitions without carefully examining their underlying assumptions or providing validation of these definitions by testing their performance in specific application settings. To address these problems, this paper proposes several formal postulates of creativity grounded in prior psychological work on creativity, especially as related to Boden's three core criteria of creativity: newness, value, and surprise. Furthermore, we propose a conceptual mathematical definition of creativity that aligns with these postulates. We also validate our proposed creativity formula in two applications: determining the creativity of particular chess moves, and assessing the creativity of paintings by some artists, such as Picasso, Renoir, and other painters. Experimental results demonstrate that our formula of creativity successfully captures creative patterns across both the chess and the art domains. This suggests that creativity can be effectively characterized through a unified mathematical structure based on three fundamental criteria, namely newness, value, and surprise, whose specific measurements are adapted to the particular domains.

items.title: Mitigating Capability Degradation in LLM Self-Improvement via Representation Geometry Regularization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mitigating Capability Degradation in LLM Self-Improvement via Representation Geometry Regularization
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-Policy Self-distillation is a self-improvement paradigm that enables large language models (LLMs) to improve their capabilities by leveraging the same model as both teacher and student under different conditioning contexts. However, we find that OPSD methods can progressively degrade previously acquired capabilities: queries that are correctly responded at earlier training stages may become incorrectly responded as optimization proceeds, even the overall performance continues to improve. Further analysis reveals that this degradation coincides with a deterioration of the geometry of hidden representations, characterized by reduced intra-cluster compactness and diminished inter-cluster separation. Motivated by this observation, we propose Representation Geometry Regularization (RGR), which preserves representation geometry during post-training by encouraging compactness within cluster and separation across cluster. RGR can be seamlessly integrated into existing OPSD methods without altering their core optimization procedures. Extensive experiments on multiple OPSD methods and benchmarks show that RGR generally alleviates capability degradation while retaining capability improvements. Our code is available in https://github.com/supermachinelearner/RGR.

items.title: Collaborative Theory of Mind: Learning to Self-Revise by Anticipating User Responses [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Collaborative Theory of Mind: Learning to Self-Revise by Anticipating User Responses
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12872v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong individual task performance, yet still struggle to collaborate with users over extended, multi-turn interactions, for example by attempting solutions before understanding the user's needs or by failing to revise mistaken assumptions after receiving feedback. We propose Collaborative Theory of Mind (CToM), a framework that addresses these challenges by explicitly training LLMs to anticipate user responses and to use those predictions to improve their own behavior. CToM drafts a response, predicts how the user will respond, and uses this prediction to guide internal revision before presenting a response. During training, the user's reply to each draft serves as the target for predicting the next turn, and we train the assistant to minimize the negative log-likelihood of that reply. We combine this prediction objective with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) to optimize both task performance and interaction efficiency. Across mathematical reasoning, coding, and writing tasks, CToM achieves higher collaborative task performance than all baselines; for example, on a collaborative mathematical reasoning task, it improves final accuracy from 74.1% to 79.6% compared with naive GRPO. Ablations show that predicting user responses also makes collaboration more efficient: under the same reward, adding prediction supervision reduces the number of user replies by 8% on coding and 17% on writing while improving task performance. Behavioral analyses of interaction trajectories show that user-response predictions become more accurate after training, and that more accurate predictions are associated with larger improvements in collaborative task performance through self-revision.

items.title: One-Step Text Generation by Seq-Drifting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: One-Step Text Generation by Seq-Drifting
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12879v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, but still require multiple sampling steps to produce high-quality text. In this paper, we investigate whether a model can learn to generate an entire sequence in a single forward pass. We propose Seq-Drifting, a framework that applies drifting to sequences of continuous token representations and directly learns a map from Gaussian noise to text. Unlike existing DLMs that derive the supervision at each position directly from the observed token in a training sequence, Seq-Drifting builds a drift field whose position-wise targets adapt to the current generated context. At each position, attraction guides each output toward a set of contextually plausible token representations, while repulsion discourages collapse across samples and repetition within sequences. The generator learns from this drift field during training and produces all tokens jointly in one pass at inference. Empirically, Seq-Drifting achieves a generative perplexity of 36.01 on LM1B in one step and performs competitively in both unconditional and conditional generation. Experiments on translation, summarization, and reasoning further demonstrate the applicability of the framework beyond open-ended generation. These results suggest that drifting over token sequences offers a promising path toward effective one-step text generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/jyliu-ai/Seq-Drifting.

items.title: Mind the Spatial Gap: A Benchmark for Geospatial Reasoning and Constrained Spatial Editing
items.originalTitle: Mind the Spatial Gap: A Benchmark for Geospatial Reasoning and Constrained Spatial Editing
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12881v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding and manipulating spatial relations is fundamental to AI systems that reason about physical environments and construct grounded world models. However, existing evaluations of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for spatial reasoning rely predominantly on static question-answering (QA) over small-scale or synthetic scenes, rarely probing whether models can modify spatial configurations while satisfying explicit geometric constraints. We introduce GeoSpatialBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate an escalating progression of spatial cognition, ranging from spatial relation understanding and geometric reasoning to constrained spatial editing. Grounded in real-world urban data across six geographically diverse cities, GeoSpatialBench evaluates a comprehensive taxonomy of 28 topological, directional, metric, and ordering relations across structured GeoJSON and map image modalities, with ground-truth references and constraints verified via GIS operations. Our empirical evaluation across frontier MLLMs uncovers a stark spatial gap: structured GeoJSON consistently outperforms map images, with multimodal combinations offering no reliable gain over GeoJSON alone, and while models show reasonable competence on qualitative topological and ordering, performance drops on quantitative metric relations. Crucially, editing performance on ordering relations declines relative to QA, and most failed edits violate at least one specified spatial constraint. These results highlight a gap between passively recognizing spatial relations and actively manipulating geometric configurations. GeoSpatialBench provides an open, rigorous diagnostic testbed to benchmark these spatial limitations, laying essential empirical groundwork for physically grounded world models and embodied spatial AI.

items.title: OGPO: Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization for Recoverable Vision-Language-Action Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OGPO: Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization for Recoverable Vision-Language-Action Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise in robotic manipulation, yet their post-training still predominantly relies on trajectory-level supervised imitation over robot demonstrations. While effective for learning feasible actions, this paradigm supervises policies to reproduce expert actions at each step, biasing them toward demonstration-specific action paths and providing limited guidance for recovering toward task-progress states once execution deviates from demonstrated trajectories. To address this limitation, we propose OGPO, an Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization framework for recoverable VLA post-training. Instead of treating offline demonstrations merely as step-wise action labels, OGPO adaptively relabels trajectories with semantic key states and constructs goal-conditioned process rewards to optimize the policy for reaching these task-progress states. In this way, OGPO shifts VLA post-training from trajectory-level action imitation to key-state reachability learning, enabling policies to acquire a more robust ability to complete goal states from feasible off-demonstration states without requiring additional online interaction. Experiments on LIBERO and MetaWorld show that OGPO consistently improves VLA policy performance over standard supervised fine-tuning. Moreover, evaluations on LIBERO-Plus and our proposed LIBERO-ReAct, a mid-execution perturbation benchmark, further demonstrate that OGPO achieves stronger robustness and goal-directed recoverability under distribution shifts and recoverable off-demonstration states.

items.title: DeFiRank: Federated Pairwise Ranking for Governance in Decentralized Financial Networks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: DeFiRank: Federated Pairwise Ranking for Governance in Decentralized Financial Networks
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing governance approaches in decentralized financial networks rely on manual review processes conducted by human committees, which introduces subjective bias, creates a scalability bottleneck under high network volume, and fails to capture complex behavioural patterns and evolving network dynamics. To address these limitations, we propose \name, a federated learning-based pairwise ranking framework in which multiple institutions collaboratively train a ranking model without sharing their private transaction data. This collaborative learning enables the model to capture network-wide behavioural patterns that signify strong network participation and directly contribute to the network effect, including diversity of counterparties, usage of multiple applications, and frequency of transactions. The proposed system ranks providers based on the authenticity of their actions, promoting genuine contributors and demoting those exhibiting suspicious behaviour. We evaluate \name\ on a real-world blockchain transaction dataset. Results demonstrate that the federated approach achieves ranking performance modestly below the centralized baseline (NDCG@15: $\approx$0.87 vs.\ $\approx$0.92) while preserving data privacy and matching its ranking stability (Kendall $\tau$: $\approx$0.70 for both regimes), producing reliable governance decisions, including provider promotion and demotion (648 and 39 unique providers, respectively), without requiring centralized access to sensitive transaction data.

items.title: AI-Mediation in Retail Markets: Revenue Effects and Assortment Optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI-Mediation in Retail Markets: Revenue Effects and Assortment Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI shopping assistants increasingly influence which products consumers consider. We study retail assortment planning under AI mediation, where a retailer chooses a catalog, an AI intermediary forms a customer-facing shortlist, and the customer chooses from that shortlist according to a multinomial logit model. We consider both deterministic mediation, in which the AI follows a fixed segment-specific ranking, and stochastic mediation based on the Plackett-Luce model. Empirically, we construct a dataset of product rankings from leading AI models, estimate Plackett-Luce ranking models, and evaluate their predictive performance on held-out assortments. Combining these estimates with synthetic customer preferences, we find that accounting for AI mediation can materially change optimal assortments and revenue. Across the tested capacity configurations, ignoring mediation yields mean revenue losses between 2.52% and 11.37% relative to the PL optimum. A much simpler deterministic plug-in, based only on the ordering of fitted AI utilities, performs substantially better, with mean losses of at most 0.53%. Motivated by this performance, we study assortment optimization under deterministic mediation. We characterize its computational complexity and show that, for any fixed number of customer segments, the problem admits a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme.

items.title: Teaching neural decoders with language [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Teaching neural decoders with language
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12921v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Brain-computer interfaces decode neural activity, yet class-label supervision (CLS) leaves relationships among classes implicit. We propose Language as Supervision (LaS), which aligns neural features with natural-language class descriptions through learned projections and predicts classes using candidate text prototypes. We evaluate seven encoder architectures with independently trained models for visual, motor, and speech decoding from scalp and intracranial recordings. LaS improves speech-decoding accuracy by up to 17.15~pp over matched CLS baselines. Its representations support candidate-set reuse and label-supervised subject and session adaptation, while LaS enables conditional unseen-frequency decoding in steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) responses. Correct class-description correspondence supports this generalization, and dual-sided attribution visualization shows neural and textual contributions to the same class-matching score. These findings suggest that text descriptions can serve as general-purpose references for learning and interpretation in neural decoding.

items.title: Collaborative Learning and Reasoning over Model Slices [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Collaborative Learning and Reasoning over Model Slices
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel across diverse tasks, benefiting from knowledge priors, in-context reasoning, and test-time computation. Despite these strengths, single-model reasoning remains vulnerable to error propagation, as later steps depend on the model's earlier outputs, leaving reasoning blind spots difficult to independently reassess. To address this limitation, we develop \textit{collaborative learning}, encompassing the construction of heterogeneous collaborators and the learning of effective cross-model collaboration. Specifically, \textit{model slicing} replaces a large model with smaller, heterogeneous models under a comparable parameter budget, enabling prior reasoning to be reassessed across distinct model parameterizations. \textit{Pyramid supervision} combines protocol distillation with step-level supervision to refine reasoning and interaction decisions throughout collaboration. We evaluate our approach across four task categories: multi-hop question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and open-ended constrained generation. The trained heterogeneous models achieve comparable or better task performance than the original large model and established multi-agent baselines, including reinforcement-learning-based methods, while also achieving higher inference efficiency than the multi-agent baselines and exhibiting differentiated collaboration patterns across tasks. These findings show that learned collaboration turns model heterogeneity into complementary reasoning capabilities.

items.title: Learning More by Training Less: Uncertainty-Guided Progressive Contraction for Efficient Reasoning Post-Training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning More by Training Less: Uncertainty-Guided Progressive Contraction for Efficient Reasoning Post-Training
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12933v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable advances in complex reasoning. However, scaling reasoning post-training with ever-larger corpora can substantially increase training cost without proportional performance gains. In this study, we therefore ask: how far can reasoning supervision be compressed without sacrificing capability? To this end, we propose an uncertainty-guided progressive contraction framework that concentrates supervision and optimization on the reasoning trajectories most valuable for learning. Specifically, rather than treating a teacher-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) as a single realized path, we construct uncertainty-profiled reasoning supervision by building Monte Carlo reasoning trees around intermediate reasoning states to expose process-level uncertainty. This uncertainty first contracts the original corpus into a compact teacher-informed pool. A second, learner-aware contraction then performs online routing during SFT, concentrating optimization according to the student's evolving learning state. Together, the two stages progressively contract both supervision and optimization, substantially reducing the student training budget. Experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks and LLM families show that our method uses as little as 0.22% of the optimization budget of full-data SFT, over 450x less training exposure, while maintaining or improving reasoning performance. Notably, our framework generalizes well across heterogeneous student families, black-box teachers, and weak-to-strong transfer. This indicates that it is not only a way to accelerate training but can also enhance reasoning capability.

items.title: MathVis: Can AI Reason through Drawing? A Benchmark for Mathematical Figure Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MathVis: Can AI Reason through Drawing? A Benchmark for Mathematical Figure Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12954v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces MathVis, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' ability to visualize frontier mathematical problems and perform diagram-assisted reasoning. The benchmark consists of 512 tasks, each comprising a mathematical statement, a reference diagram, executable TikZ or SVG code, a Gold Intermediate Representation (IR), atomic rubrics, and error codes. Through rigorous evaluation, GPT-6-Astra, Claude Fable 5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve pass@1 scores of 31.25%, 26.56%, and 22.85%, respectively. We found that although the tasks require visualization, LLMs produce outputs dominated by formal languages, symbols, and graphics programs, rather than explicit diagram-mediated reasoning. Furthermore, while the solutions generated by LLMs may contain all the necessary elements, they are often visually confusing to humans. Ultimately, this benchmark aims to visualize mathematical problems and promote research on enabling LLMs to simplify their reasoning via visual diagrams.

items.title: SmartSalesBench: A Resistance-Aware Multi-Turn Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Sales Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SmartSalesBench: A Resistance-Aware Multi-Turn Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Sales Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present SmartSalesBench, the first multi-turn conversational benchmark explicitly designed to evaluate large language model (LLM) sales agents against psychologically grounded, resistant buyer personas. Existing task-oriented dialogue benchmarks assume cooperative users and measure task completion; SmartSalesBench inverts this assumption, placing agents against personas programmed to resist and challenge across conversations of up to twenty turns. The benchmark includes five agent profiles, twelve buyer personas, fifteen smartphone products across six price tiers, and four controlled experiments with 3 iterations totaling 13,680 sessions. Both sales-agent and buyer persona generations are grounded through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We introduce nine evaluation metrics grouped into three tiers: primary outcome metrics (CR, BRS, RIR), secondary quality metrics (SMS, PFS, ETI), and exploratory metrics planned for future reporting (ITS, ARI, SPI). Our evaluation combines automated LLM-as-judge scoring with internal human assessment (n = 50, \k{appa} = 0.71, Pearson r = 0.81 with BRS).

items.title: Beyond Semantic IDs: Finite-Beam Reachability and Continuous-Query Generation in Generative Recommendation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Semantic IDs: Finite-Beam Reachability and Continuous-Query Generation in Generative Recommendation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) of social media platforms commonly retrieves items by autoregressively decoding discrete Semantic IDs (SIDs) with finite-width beam search. This work examines how this output interface constrains whether held-out targets enter finite returned lists, while distinguishing catalog-wide scoreability from empirical top-K support. We introduce two continuous-query paradigms: CQG-Single generates one retrieval query in a single pass, and CQG-AR autoregressively generates continuous residual updates, retaining step-wise decoding while removing the SID item-token vocabulary, code lookup, and discrete beam expansion. These designs thereby eliminate the SID-specific reachability constraint induced by finite-beam decoding and avoid the technical challenge of aligning a discrete SID vocabulary with the pretrained backbone's vector space. Both methods make every encoded item directly scoreable through dense or approximate-nearest-neighbor retrieval. Under a unified protocol with valid-prefix constrained decoding, CQG-Single exceeds the TIGER-style baseline in all seven runs while using 55.3% as many trainable parameters. CQG-AR remains comparable on ML-1M and is numerically stronger on Beauty and Sports datasets. A controlled depth ablation further shows that additional continuous refinement does not monotonically improve shallow accuracy. These findings motivate decoupling output representation, autoregressive modeling, and retrieval budget when evaluating generative recommendation systems.

items.title: Work2Skill: Capturing Human GUI Experience for Reusable Agent Skill Induction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Work2Skill: Capturing Human GUI Experience for Reusable Agent Skill Induction
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computer-use agents can perform increasingly complex GUI tasks, yet unfamiliar software and workflows requiring human domain knowledge remain challenging. Human demonstrations convey procedural knowledge through the same GUI interaction space, but reuse requires interpreting actions in context and separating workflow rules from task-specific details. We thus introduce Work2Skill, a framework that captures human GUI experience for reusable agent skill induction. WorkRecorder provides the framework's infrastructure for collecting this experience, aligning screen recordings, mouse and keyboard events, and available accessibility-tree information. Using WorkRecorder, we construct WorkDemo-350, the first synchronized multimodal dataset of human desktop GUI demonstrations for reusable agent skill induction and downstream evaluation. Its 350 demonstrations are screened for completeness and task success. We then propose an agentic skill-induction method that inspects evidence on demand to produce reusable skills capturing workflow rules, step dependencies, and completion checks. When the same four execution models are equipped with skills induced by each method under shared execution settings, Work2Skill achieves the highest scores and success rates. Mean score improvements over the corresponding No Skill baseline are 4.67--10.54 points on MyPCBench Bounded Action and 3.11--7.50 points on a 286-task subset of OSWorld-Verified. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/china-qijizhifeng/Work2Skill.

items.title: Benchmarking Embedding Geometries and Clustering Algorithms for Unsupervised Patent Claim Classification [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Benchmarking Embedding Geometries and Clustering Algorithms for Unsupervised Patent Claim Classification
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prior-art retrieval systems are structurally organized around classification codes, making cross-code discovery difficult. This paper asks if an unsupervised representation trained on patent text can recover relevant connections that code-restricted search cannot, and if hyperbolic space helps. We trained a hyperbolic and a matched Euclidean Variational Autoencoder (VAE) on 45,000 US patents (96 runs, 6 seeds). The hyperbolic model retrieves genuinely cross-category prior art 52% more often than the Euclidean model (18.76% vs. 12.34% of top-10 results, 3,000 queries). This represents a practical gain for the motivating search problem. The hyperbolic model agrees less with official classification (NMI 0.2392 vs. 0.3206), which we explain geometrically: the two measures capture different goals, and only one aligns with prior-art search needs. In a study of 10 technology domains (50,000 more patents), we find that a domain's classification breadth--the number of distinct CPC subgroups spanned--predicts approach performance (Pearson r=-0.642, p=0.045, N=10), and that patents per subgroup is an even stronger predictor (r=0.715, p=0.020). This provides a checkable signal for practitioners to determine where the method is most valuable. We report all findings with statistical transparency and release a complete, 91-test automated implementation.

items.title: Hindsight Structured Advice Distillation: Steering Executor Agents with Advisors Trained on Their Failures and Task Characteristics [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Hindsight Structured Advice Distillation: Steering Executor Agents with Advisors Trained on Their Failures and Task Characteristics
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13000v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-model agents are used for specialized work such as financial research, healthcare and law. Such agents are often capable enough for a task but still miss its details. In finance, for example, these details include which filing reports a figure or how a company discloses a metric. Retraining the agent to learn these details is expensive, and often impossible when the agent is a closed or shared system. Writing the missing know-how into the agent's prompt makes the prompt long and identical for every input, although different inputs need different guidance. We propose to learn to generate this guidance instead. A small advisor model reads each input and writes structured advice, which is appended to the prompt of a frozen executor. The advisor is trained with hindsight, following work on distillation with privileged information. On a training pool with graded answers, we analyse the executor's failures, run it under several strategies to see which one worked on each input, and let a teacher that sees the grades and the traces write the advice that would have helped. The advisor then learns, by supervised fine-tuning, to write that advice from the input alone. Because the student is a separate small model rather than the executor, it is cheap to train and adds little latency. We call this approach hindsight structured advice distillation (HSAD). On FrontierFinance, a public benchmark of expert-written financial research queries, an 8B advisor raises the qualification rate of Samaya's proprietary research agent, which already leads the benchmark's leaderboard, from 52.9% to 56.6%. This is above the agent's own high-effort configuration, at 37% lower cost per query. We study the generalization of the proposed approach, and in particular show that HSAD also improves results on WebShop, BIRD text-to-SQL and ExpertLongBench.

items.title: Scaling Empowered Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Scaling Empowered Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Empowerment measures the capacity of an agent to actively control its environment. In this work, we explain the connection between skill learning and empowerment. While skill learning is not empowerment, we introduce a simple scalable recipe for empowerment maximization: empowerment corresponds to the number of executable skills from a state, so maximizing empowerment corresponds to reaching states that are good starting points for many skills. Our recipe applies to arbitrary underlying skill learning methods. Whereas most prior work on empowerment looks at tabular settings, this recipe enables us to study empowerment at a scale where we can realize theoretically-predicted but empirically-elusive properties of empowerment (e.g., gathering resources, environment modification, survival). Experiments show that empowerment maximization unlocks interesting emergent properties, such as building a house in Crafter. Website and code at \href{https://empowerment-geometry.github.io/scaling-empowerment/}{this https url}.

items.title: Provenance-Aware Belief Updating in Human-AI Feedback Loops [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Provenance-Aware Belief Updating in Human-AI Feedback Loops
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In repeated human-AI interaction, a single observation can be quoted, summarized, and returned to a model as multiple reports, making repetition look like independent corroboration. We study whether language models can use supplied report lineage to update according to evidence provenance rather than report count. We introduce Latent Quotient Evidence Training (LQET), a relational objective that combines sparse Bayesian supervision with constraints that encourage stable predictions when reports add no new evidence and consistent updates to the same new evidence across relay histories. On a controlled binary benchmark, LQET reduces new-evidence update RMSE by 41-44% and log-odds drift after eight relay steps by 89-91% relative to task-only training across Qwen3-4B and Phi-4-mini, with three paired training seeds per backbone. The gains extend to a closed-loop simulation in which model confidence controls how many relayed reports re-enter the model's context in later rounds. By grounding belief updates in supplied provenance, LQET offers a route toward dynamic human-AI systems in which influence follows new evidence, not the number of times the same evidence returns.

items.title: EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continual learning requires models to accumulate past experience and transfer it to new tasks. Despite substantial research on continual learning, existing work remains largely confined to non-embodied settings, without extending to embodied environments. To address this gap, we introduce EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark in embodied simulation for evaluating the continual learning capability of self-evolving agents. With compositional generalization as the core evaluation principle, our benchmark evaluates whether agents can first learn from basic tasks and then recombine the acquired skills to solve complex, unseen advanced tasks. Based on EmbodiedCLBench, we conduct extensive experiments across multiple agent harnesses and learning methods, revealing consistent limitations and distinctive behaviors. Our results show that while advanced tasks can be hardly solved under zero-shot setting, the experience from basic tasks enables consistent improvement. Such benefit from the experience remains stable even if the task complexity increases. However, this improvement does not scale accordingly with the number of learning samples, and current agents cannot extract meaningful information from additional experience. Collectively, our findings highlight continual learning as a fundamental yet underexplored capability, and our benchmark offers valuable resources for designing effective self-evolving agents in embodied environments. Our code and dataset are available at https://pku-value-lab.github.io/EmbodiedCLBench-homepage.

items.title: Travel Back To Move Forward: Retrospective Exploration and Evolving for Long Horizon Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Travel Back To Move Forward: Retrospective Exploration and Evolving for Long Horizon Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13058v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly operate in long-horizon environments where early mistakes can trigger cascading failures and trap agents in dead-end trajectories. Agents must therefore be able to proactively recover from such states and turn their exploratory experience into guidance for subsequent decisions. We introduce ReTRAIL, a framework that enables agents to rewind the environment to earlier states while preserving valid progress and carrying forward knowledge learned from abandoned exploration. The environment state moves backward while the agent's knowledge continues to move forward. ReTRAIL trains a shared policy with two complementary signals: State-Anchored GRPO compares alternative continuations from revisited states to improve execution, while a branch-advancement reward guides reflection through the progress of subsequent exploration.
